Month 9. Monday morning. The new institute's website stopped loading.
Enquiry forms down. Parent emails bouncing.

The domain had expired on Saturday. Every renewal reminder went to the personal inbox of the staff member who set it up. She had left in month 4.

So the team went looking for everything else that renews.

They found 14 items in year one: 
→ Building lease 
→ Fire safety NOC 
→ Insurance 
→ LMS and email licences 
→ Domain and hosting 
→ Generator and AC maintenance contracts ...and 8 more.

Only 5 had a date written down anywhere. 3 were still in the name of people who had left.

Nobody was careless. Setup months are a blur of approvals, hiring and fit-outs. Papers get signed, filed and forgotten. Until one lapses.

The fix is a setup register, written before opening day:
→ Every licence, approval and contract on one sheet 
→ A renewal date and one named owner for each 
→ A reminder 60 days out, sent to a role inbox, not a person.

That register is part of how we set up new institutes in our New Institutional 
Setup work. Openings get celebrated. Renewals keep the doors open.

Opening an institute this year? List what renews before you cut the ribbon.
(Story and figures are an illustrative composite, not a real institute.)

Follow AAS Eduguide for more on building institutions that run well from day one.

My speech for the graduates of 2026:

Good evening game development students, class of 2026, and let me also congratulate you on graduating from Digital Arts and Entertainment.
This speech is difficult for me and I am also nervous, because we must talk about the future. There is an elephant in the room here this evening and it is off course artificial intelligence. I trust that everybody has heard enough about AI the last few weeks and months and is perhaps even sick of it. Social media is full of articles about AI and how it is transforming the workplace. 
But before we hop on the bandwagon perhaps it is appropriate to reflect on the impact AI has on society.
Perhaps it is not a good idea to ditch 60,000 people from your workforce, unless you want your product to be called Microsoft 364.
Perhaps it is not a good idea to hand over critical software over to AI, lest you want to ground your planes for half a day.
Perhaps it is also not a good idea for Belgian schools and universities to fill the coffers of U.S. companies such as Microsoft and OpenAI via public funding which is ultimately paid for by taxpayers. Even more so when the ethics of those companies with regards to the social contract is questionable.
As a coordinator of a small university of a small country, all I can do is raise my voice. But perhaps if enough of use raise our voices we can be heard. 
And it IS important as there is a lot of uncertainty for our freshmen, enrolled students and graduates. It used to be customary that students questioned certain subjects or courses in a study program. But a much more pernicious question is rearing its head: “Why study anything at all? Why practice anything at all ?”  
From our point of view as a technical university we offer formation. We develop skills and knowledge. I would argue that a broad and foundational knowledge is even more important in the current era. My message to students and graduates is clear: domain knowledge and skills ARE important, let nobody tell you otherwise. It may be the case that you arrive at a game studio where the use of AI is permitted, or even obligatory. But the skills you developed here and the knowledge that you have is what will carry your professional life.
There is a saying that it takes a village to raise a child. I carry that over to game development: “It takes a village to create a game”. You need people from all walks of life, of all ages and backgrounds to create a successful game. Not hiring juniors as a shortsighted way to save cost is penny wise and pound foolish. The new generation needs the opportunity to grow by making the mistakes we all made when we started out as professionals.
Players want games created by humans, for humans. We want to hear stories that were written by humans and immerse ourself in fictional worlds that evoke a meaningful experience. I am convinced that this generation of freshly graduated game developers can bring that experience with or without AI.

A general AI tool used for staff decisions may make you its provider.

Imagine a head of operations at a 2,500-person logistics firm. Team leaders paste shift notes into the company's general AI assistant. They ask it to rank staff for overtime and promotion. The vendor sold the tool for drafting and summarising, and its terms rule out high-risk uses. Nobody in HR or procurement knows.

Call it purpose drift: the tool's stated purpose stays put while its real use moves. Under EU law, for firms within the AI Act's reach, the provider is the party that carries the maker's duties. Article 25 of the AI Act treats a deployer as the provider in three cases. One is when it changes the intended purpose of an AI system, a general-purpose one included, so that it becomes high-risk. Decisions on promotion, task allocation based on individual behaviour and the evaluation of staff performance are on the high-risk list.

The Commission's draft guidelines on classification, issued on 19 May 2026, repeat this warning for deployers. The final version is due by the end of 2026. The AI Omnibus (Regulation 2026/1744) moved the high-risk rules for these uses to 2 December 2027. ONS found 55% of employees in Great Britain using AI for work or education in May and June 2026. Only 35% of UK businesses with 10 or more employees reported AI use. The employee figure may include some AI use outside formal business activities. The Act also adds a catch. Suppose a vendor has clearly said its tool must not become a high-risk system. It then need not hand over the documentation a new provider would need.

Three steps. Ask every AI vendor to state in writing which uses it excludes. Keep a list of what staff really use each tool for, and who decides. Route any use that touches hiring, pay, promotion or task allocation through one named approver. A tool used that way needs a different contract, not a different prompt.

If nobody can say what staff really use your general AI tools for, we start there.

A good AI contractor can bill £1,200 a day. That's about £264k a year. Your £150k permanent offer just became a pay cut.

UK demand for IT contractors is at its highest in 44 months. The REC's temporary technology staff index hit 53.7 in September, the strongest reading since January 2023, and AI is a big part of what's driving it. Day rates for AI experience are running from about £750 to £1,200, and in one set of approaches tracked for ContractorUK, 53% of AI roles were outside IR35.

So if you're hiring a permanent Head of AI or Director this quarter, the person you want can often earn more, with more freedom, by staying on the contract side.

Three things that actually help:

1. Lead with scope, not job title. Senior people move for a clear mandate and a reporting line that can unblock budget.
2. Move fast. Good AI contractors are in several conversations at once. Three weeks from first chat to offer is how you lose them.
3. Be honest about what permanent pays for. Security, influence, a team to build. If your package can't beat six months outside IR35 on cash alone, stop pretending it can and sell what it can.

Permanent still wins when the role is real. It loses when the brief is vague and the process is slow.

LLM & AI Agent testing series - Post 5 of 5: The release gate

Testing an AI agent only counts if it can stop a bad release.

Here’s the pipeline I’d put in front of any LLM application:

Component checks: parsers, routers, tool schemas, prompt contracts
Offline evals on a versioned dataset
Trajectory checks for wrong tools, wrong order, missing approvals, loops
Performance budgets for latency, cost, tokens and retries
Safety checks: code catches the unambiguous rules (PII patterns, forbidden calls), experts review the judgment calls
Human sign-off on anything sensitive or high-risk
Then production traces feed back into the dataset, and the loop repeats.

None of this is new to me. It’s shift-left quality gates, the same model I’ve applied in Azure DevOps pipelines on data platform and ERP programmes, pointed at a new kind of system.

That’s why I built my AI Test Pilot with the Claude API and Playwright

I was talking to a SaaS founder the other day.

He firmly believes AI can do marketing, and that one person is enough to run the whole function. His logic: you fill the AI with your thoughts, and the rest gets taken care of. 

Then, at the end of the conversation, he told me he’s hiring someone to look after marketing. Someone who can bring in “leads.”

That made me pause.

If AI can handle the entire marketing function, why hire anyone at all?

Maybe the answer is simpler than it looks. You can’t fire an AI tool because the leads didn’t come in. You can hold a person accountable for it.

I don’t say this to be cynical. I say it because I keep seeing the same pattern. Founders want marketing to be fast, automated, and fully predictable, but they still want a human name next to the outcome.

Here’s the reality. AI can speed up execution. It can’t own a positioning decision, read a market shift, or build trust with a buyer who is about to sign a large contract. Those parts of marketing still need judgment, context, and someone who understands the product deeply.

And leads are an outcome, not a task. They come from clear positioning, a sharp narrative, consistent content, and the right distribution. Hiring one person to “bring in leads” without fixing those foundations is not a marketing strategy. It’s a hope.

If you’re a founder, be honest about what you’re actually buying: a tool, or an owner for the outcome. Because those are two very different decisions.

A first move we often see in AI governance is buying an ISO/IEC 42001 certification project. In our view it is usually the wrong first move.

Not because the standard is wrong. Because certification scopes what you already know, and many organisations do not yet know what AI they run.

Build the inventory first. Then let it choose the starting point:

• Mostly bought or embedded AI? Your risk sits with suppliers. Start with third-party controls and contract clauses.

• Systems that decide on credit, hiring, benefits or the public? Start with risk classification. The EU AI Act's Annex III categories are a useful lens even outside the EU.

• Mostly staff productivity tools? Start with an acceptable-use policy and AI literacy. Certification can wait.

One more reason to be precise: for providers selling high-risk AI into the EU, ISO/IEC 42001 on its own does not give a presumption of conformity under the AI Act. Since October, the harmonised standard EN 18286:2026 does, for the quality-management part (Articles 11(1) and 17(1)).

A good inventory makes every later step cheaper. The scope statement, the NIST MAP function, the EU classification all begin with the same question: what is in scope?

The 2026 State of Data Engineering report, based on over 1,000 responses, confirms a shift I have been feeling in production for the last six months: the era of the generalist data engineer is ending, and the era of the specialized workflow engineer is beginning.

The non-obvious insight from the data is not that AI is replacing jobs. It is that AI is collapsing the distance between idea and deployment, which changes the skill that matters most. The scarce resource in 2026 is no longer the ability to write a pipeline. It is the ability to design the guardrails, fallback chains, and validation gates that make autonomous pipeline generation safe. Every team I see struggling is not struggling because their AI agents are not powerful enough. They are struggling because they have not defined the operational contract that the agent must satisfy before it can deploy.

Another structural change the report highlights is the maturation of platform-owned infrastructure. The winning pattern is no longer a centralized data team serving every business unit. It is a platform team that provides the enforcement layer—cost budgets, schema validation, compliance rules—while individual teams own their pipelines. This is a fundamental shift in organizational design that most hiring processes still do not account for.

The most under-discussed trend is the rise of event-driven pipelines as the default architecture, not a niche pattern. The report confirms that teams are moving away from batch-first designs, not because batch is bad, but because the cost of latency is now higher than the cost of complexity. The teams winning are the ones who treat every event as a governed object from ingress to egress, not as a file to be processed later.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to build a single pipeline or tune a specific tool. I am seeking a problem where I can design the governance layer, the fallback strategies, and the organizational patterns that make a team's pipeline output predictable as it scales. If your organization is adopting AI for pipeline generation but struggling to enforce cost or quality policies, or if your data platform is growing but your team's delivery velocity is flat, I want to hear about the specific autonomy levels and governance gaps you are navigating.

What is the one operational contract in your current pipeline environment that, if enforced before any code is deployed, would eliminate your most common production incident?

Is a permanent job becoming a luxury?

For a generation, "permanent" was the word that made a job real. The salary you could plan around. The loan you could sign. The parent you could reassure.

Mint analysed 353 BSE 500 companies last week. Non-permanent employees, meaning fixed-term, contract and gig workers, made up 17% of their workforce in FY26. Three years earlier, it was about 11%.

One in six. At India's largest listed companies.

From the business side, the logic holds. Demand is volatile, AI is rewriting roles, costs keep rising. Flexibility is rational.

But flexibility is not free. It is simply paid for by someone else.

A fixed-term contract does not remove uncertainty. It moves it from the balance sheet to a household.

The home loan runs twenty years. The contract runs twelve months.

I am not arguing against flexible hiring. I am arguing against pretending it costs nothing.

If a business needs flexibility, it can pay for it. A premium on the rate. Notice that is real. A path to permanent that is written down, not implied.

Are we building a more flexible workforce, or a less secure generation?

One job. Two companies. Six professions. Multiple languages. And a one-minute WhatsApp audition! 😄

I came across an interesting job advertisement on LinkedIn. This job was posted on LinkedIn yesterday for a company headquartered in Dubai. 
The designation? Business Operations Specialist.
 
The person needs to be a lawyer, since they’ll handle contracts, resolutions and corporate structuring. They also need to be an accountant, since they’ll deal with bookkeeping, VAT and Corporate Tax. They’ll be a PRO, running visas, attestations and renewals with the authorities. They’ll be a client relationship manager for international clients. And on top of that, they’re expected to build AI workflows and prepare leadership reports.
 
Languages? Excellent English, German as a strong plus, and every extra language adds value. Because speaking German is apparently a “nice to have” now.
 
Then comes my favourite part. You also have to send a one-minute WhatsApp video introducing yourself. Be creative. Show your energy.
 
So the shortlist is a lawyer, an accountant, a compliance officer, an operations manager, an AI enthusiast and a camera-ready linguist. With 2 to 4 years of experience!!!
 
I’m all for versatility and ownership. I’ve worked with people who can juggle a lot, and they’re gold. But when one role covers this many professions, it’s fair to ask whether we’re hiring a person or a whole department.
 
Here’s a thought. Instead of asking one human to wear ten hats, build an AI operations assistant for the repeatable work first. Documentation, compliance reminders, workflow tracking, routine client updates and report drafts are all things AI can already handle well.
 
Then hire a person for what needs judgement, relationships and accountability. That’s where people matter most.
 
Because the best addition to your team might not need a CV, a German certificate or a WhatsApp audition.
 
So here’s my question. Are we writing job descriptions faster than we’re rethinking how the work gets done?

🌐 GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE…
Most developers learn HTTP methods like this:
GET → Read
POST → Create
PUT → Update
DELETE → Delete
Useful? Yes.
Complete? Not really.

HTTP methods communicate the intent and semantics of a request.
And once you're designing APIs, understanding those semantics matters.

Here are some HTTP methods every developer should understand:
01 — GET
Retrieve a resource.
GET /users/42
GET should be safe and shouldn't intentionally modify server state.
02 — POST
Submit data or trigger processing.
POST /users
Commonly used for creating resources—but creation isn't its only purpose.
03 — PUT
Replace the representation of a resource at a known URI.
PUT /users/42
Think:
“Make this resource look like this.”
04 — PATCH
Apply a partial modification.
PATCH /users/42
Useful when only a few fields need changing.
05 — DELETE
Request removal of a resource.
DELETE /users/42
An important detail:
Deleting the same resource twice shouldn't produce additional state changes.
06 — HEAD
Similar to GET, but the server returns headers without the response body.
Useful for checking metadata or resource availability without transferring the representation.
07 — OPTIONS
Ask what communication options are available for a resource/server.
You'll often encounter it around CORS preflight requests.
08 — CONNECT
Establish a tunnel through a proxy.
Commonly associated with HTTPS proxying.
09 — TRACE
Performs a diagnostic loop-back of the request.

Rarely used in normal application APIs and often disabled for security reasons.
But knowing the method name isn't enough.

Two concepts make HTTP semantics much easier to understand:
Safe

A safe method is intended to be read-only.
GET
HEAD
OPTIONS
TRACE
Idempotent

Sending the same request multiple times should have the same intended effect on server state as sending it once.

Typically:
GET ✅
PUT ✅
DELETE ✅
HEAD ✅
OPTIONS ✅
POST ❌ generally not
PATCH ⚠️ depends on the patch semantics

This distinction becomes extremely important when you introduce:
→ retries
→ distributed systems
→ API gateways
→ unreliable networks
→ background jobs
→ payment APIs
If a request times out, can the client safely retry it?

That question is often more important than simply asking:
“Should I use POST or PUT?”

HTTP methods aren't just verbs attached to URLs.

They are contracts between clients, servers and infrastructure.

What HTTP concept should be next: status codes, headers, REST API design, or idempotency keys?

32,000+ hours on Upwork. How would I get my first contract today?

After my last post, I received many reactions and messages. Some shared their experiences; others asked how I completed 150+ contracts and how they could land their first one.

Thank you for every message!

But first, something important.

The Upwork I started on is not the Upwork we have today.

Now freelancers pay Connects, compete with boosted proposals, and face hundreds of applications, many written by AI.

Being a good specialist doesn't even guarantee that a client will see your proposal.

So I won't pretend that what worked for me years ago is a magic formula today.

But if I had to start from zero, here's what I'd do.

1. Sell a solution, not a list of skills.
"I can automate your critical business flows with Playwright" sounds much better than "I'm experienced in manual and automated testing."
Clients have problems. Show them how you can solve those problems.

2. Build a portfolio before getting reviews.
No Upwork history? Build something yourself. Publish it on GitHub, record a short demo, or write a case study.
Real work speaks louder than a long list of technologies.

3. Don't waste Connects.
Check the client's hiring history, budget, and project description.
I'd rather send five thoughtful proposals than fifty generic ones. And I certainly wouldn't boost every application.

4. Write like a human being.
Forget those long introductions about being passionate, hardworking, and detail-oriented.
Explain how you'd approach the problem. Share one relevant example. Ask a useful question.
AI can help with grammar, but don't let it replace your personality.

5. Start small, but don't work for free.
A small automation task, QA audit, or bug investigation can be a great first contract.
Your time has value, even without reviews.

6. Think beyond the first contract.
Here's something from my own experience.
My very first Upwork client and I continued working together, on and off, for five years.
Sometimes we had new projects. Sometimes months passed without any work. But the trust remained.
That's something beginners often underestimate.
You don't need hundreds of clients to build a successful freelance career. A few long-term relationships can be worth much more than dozens of one-time contracts.

7. Don't depend entirely on Upwork.
Build your LinkedIn network. Share your work. Ask satisfied clients for referrals.
A platform should help your career, not become your entire career.
And finally, I know how frustrating it is to have the skills, spend money applying, and receive absolutely no response.
There's no guaranteed formula for success, especially in today's market.
But I still believe that real expertise, clear communication, and trust are worth more than a perfectly polished AI-generated proposal.

32,000 hours didn't happen overnight. And there was no magic trick.

As the Cost of Doing Business (CODB) is increasing year after year and 2nd marging is reducing due to increase in competition and global volatility etc - to reduce the  high overheads and  HR cost of  highly paid traditional mid and top level  Management Committee (ManCom) employees,  India Inc. and Globally Big Corporates are increasingly using "indirect layoffs"—Replacing permanent roles with independent consultants, gig workers, and contract staff, freelancers —to bypass long-term statutory liabilities like Retirement  overheads and obligation of time bound promotions  increments during the employment periods while adapting to rapid AI-driven tech shifts. According to an analysis reported by Mint, non-permanent employees across 353 BSE 500 companies jumped from roughly 11% in FY23 to 17% in FY26.
While this structural shift gives companies operational agility, India's new labour codes—effective November 21, 2025—have significantly tightened the legal loopholes around how these workers are classified and compensated.

1. Why Companies Are Shifting to Consultants

• Bypassing Statutory Liabilities. Engaging independent consultants on a business-to-business (B2B) or retainer basis removes the employer's obligation to pay the 12% employer PF contribution, Gratuity, Time bound promotions, Pension, high premium of  Medical Insurances  , and paid leave benefits as per last salary package rates, Training time cost salary and inadequate skill capabilities  to adopt the new technology due to mid-aged  and blocked mindsets of employees of these positions.
• Tech & AI Agility. Rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence and automation have shortened the shelf life of traditional corporate skills. Companies prefer hiring specialized consultants for specific transformation projects rather than carrying permanent headcount that requires costly upskilling or formal retrenchment.
• Avoiding Retrenchment Friction. Under the Industrial Relations Code, formal layoffs and retrenchments require strict notice periods, severance compensation (15 days' average pay per year of service), and government approval for larger establishments. Letting a consultant's contract expire avoids both legal friction and negative publicity.
